notes.title: Rotor Systems
notes.subtitle: A two-blade teetering main rotor with coning hinges and droop stops, oil-filled sealed pitch-change bearing housings, and a stainless-steel leading-edge spar the paint must protect at the skin-to-spar bond line.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Rotor Systems).

sections.heading: Main rotor
paragraphs: Two all-metal blades mounted to the hub by coning hinges, the hub mounted to the shaft by a teeter hinge — both hinges on self-lubricated bearings. Droop stops give the teeter hinge a friction restraint that normally keeps the rotor from teetering while stopping or starting. Each blade's pitch-change bearings are enclosed in a housing at the blade root, filled with oil and sealed with an elastomeric boot.

Each blade has a thick stainless-steel spar at the leading edge, resistant to corrosion and erosion, with the skins bonded to the spar about one inch aft of the leading edge. Blades must be refinished if the paint erodes to bare metal at the skin-to-spar bond line — the bond can be damaged if that bond line is exposed.

sections.heading: Tail rotor
paragraphs: Two all-metal blades on a teetering hub with a fixed coning angle. The pitch-change bearings have self-lubricated liners; the teeter-hinge bearings are elastomeric or have self-lubricated liners. The blades are built with aluminium skins and root fittings, and maintaining the paint finish reduces corrosion and erosion.

notes.title: Drive System
notes.subtitle: Vee-belts from an engine-shaft sheave to an upper sheave that carries the overrunning clutch, then one shaft forward to the main rotor and aft to the tail rotor, with a splash-lubricated single-stage main gearbox on four rubber mounts.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Drive System).

sections.heading: Engine to rotors
paragraphs: A vee-belt sheave is bolted directly to the engine output shaft. Vee-belts transmit power to the upper sheave, which has an overrunning (sprag) clutch in its hub; the clutch's inner shaft drives forward to the main rotor and aft to the tail rotor. Flexible couplings sit at the main gearbox input and at each end of the long tail rotor drive shaft.

The main gearbox is a single-stage spiral-bevel gear set, splash-lubricated, cooled by a duct under the gearbox connected to the top of the engine shroud, and supported by four rubber mounts. The long tail rotor drive shaft has no support bearings but has a lightly-loaded damper bearing; the tail gearbox is a single 90° splash-lubricated spiral-bevel set.

notes.title: Powerplant
notes.subtitle: One carbureted Lycoming four-cylinder — horizontally opposed, air-cooled, wet-sump — with a shaft-driven cooling fan and a carburetor air box fed cool or warm air by a pilot-controlled sliding valve.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Powerplant); Sections 1 and 2 for specifications and limitations.

sections.heading: The engine
paragraphs: One Lycoming four-cylinder, horizontally-opposed, overhead-valve, air-cooled, carbureted engine with a wet-sump oil system. It is equipped with a starter, an alternator, shielded ignition, two magnetos, a muffler, an oil cooler, and an induction air filter. A direct-drive squirrel-cage fan on the engine output shaft supplies cooling air to the cylinders and oil cooler through a fibreglass and aluminium shroud.

Induction air enters through an inlet on the right side of the fuselage and passes through a flexible duct to the carburetor air box. A hot-air scoop supplies heated air to the box, and a pilot-controlled sliding valve lets either cool or warm air flow into the box, through the air filter, and up into the carburetor.

notes.title: Flight Controls, Trim and Friction
notes.subtitle: Unboosted push-pull-tube controls — no hydraulics — with a collective-up spring that balances the rotor loads, a fixed longitudinal cyclic bungee, and an on-off lateral trim spring reached around the left of the cyclic post so it is not confused with the mixture.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Flight Controls, Removable Flight Controls, Control Trim and Friction).

sections.heading: The controls
paragraphs: Dual controls are standard, all actuated through push-pull tubes and bellcranks on sealed ball bearings or self-lubricated liners — there is no hydraulic boost. The cyclic is centre-mounted, the two grips on a cross tube that pivots on the centre post; on later aircraft a mechanic can adjust the pilot's grip angle. The collective is conventional, with the engine throttle correlated to it through a mechanical linkage (raise opens the throttle, lower closes it) plus a twist-grip throttle on each collective stick. Left-seat cyclic grip, collective and pedals can be removed with quick-release pins.

Above 4,000 ft, throttle-collective correlation and the governor are both less effective, so power changes should be slow and smooth, and at high power above 4,000 ft the throttle is often wide open and RPM must be controlled with collective.

sections.heading: Trim springs
paragraphs: Balancing trim springs are built into the cyclic and collective. The collective-up spring balances the rotor loads so the pilot can take the left hand off the collective in most flight regimes. The longitudinal cyclic has a fixed bungee spring that cancels most longitudinal stick force in cruise. The lateral cyclic has an on-off trim spring that cancels the left stick force in high-speed flight, actuated by a push-pull knob just forward of the cyclic stick (with fine adjustment on the left console for S/N 550 and later).
sections.note: Reach around the left side of the cyclic centre post to actuate the lateral trim — if the mixture control is pulled by mistake in flight, the engine will stop.

sections.heading: Friction
paragraphs: Cyclic and collective have adjustable friction devices: a collective friction lever near the aft end of the pilot's collective (aft to increase, forward to release) and a cyclic friction knob left of the centre post (clockwise applies friction to both longitudinal and lateral cyclic). The pedals connect directly to the tail rotor pitch control and have no trim spring or friction device. Control friction must be used with caution in flight — excessive friction can make the helicopter difficult to control.

notes.title: RPM Governor and Engine Controls
notes.subtitle: A friction-clutch governor that only works above 80% engine RPM and can be flown through, the overtravel spring for run-on autorotations, carburetor heat, and the optional cold-start primer.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — RPM Governor, Engine Controls, Engine Primer System).

sections.heading: The RPM governor
paragraphs: The governor maintains engine RPM by sensing changes and applying corrective throttle inputs through a friction clutch that the pilot can easily override. It is active only above 80% engine RPM and is switched on or off by a toggle on the end of the right-seat collective. It assists under normal conditions but may not prevent over- or under-speed from aggressive manoeuvres, and at high density altitude its response rate may be too slow to prevent an overspeed during gusts, pull-ups or when lowering collective.

sections.heading: Engine controls
paragraphs: Interconnected twist-grip throttles on both collectives actuate the throttle valve through a mechanical linkage, and the electronic governor makes minor throttle adjustments by rotating the twist grip within power-on limits — manual manipulation is normally only needed for start-up, shutdown, autorotation practice and emergencies. An overtravel spring in the throttle linkage lets the pilot roll the throttle off beyond the idle stop before a ground-contact (run-on) autorotation landing, so the throttle does not open when the collective is raised — its adjustment is checked on preflight by rolling the twist grip through the overtravel spring against the idle stop and confirming the carburetor throttle arm just starts to move as the collective is raised full up.

Other engine controls are a mixture control (forward and to the right of the cyclic centre post, or on the console face on some aircraft) and a carburetor heat control (right and aft of the cyclic); R22s with the O-360 engine have Carb Heat Assist, described in Section 4. In-flight leaning with the mixture control is not recommended, and mixture leaned on the ground at high altitude must be pushed back in before descending or the engine may quit.
sections.note: The optional engine primer improves cold starting: a primer pump in front of the right seat near the hourmeter is unlocked and pumped (normally two to three strokes, pulling up slowly to let fuel fill the pump), then pushed full down and locked before start.

notes.title: Clutch Actuator
notes.subtitle: The electric actuator that raises the upper drive sheave to tension the vee-belts after start — and the clutch caution light that stays on the whole time it is working.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Clutch Actuator).

sections.heading: What it does
paragraphs: After the engine starts it is coupled to the rotor drive system through vee-belts tensioned by raising the upper drive sheave. An electric actuator between the sheaves raises the upper sheave when the pilot engages the clutch switch; it senses compressive load (belt tension) and switches off when the belts are properly tensioned. The clutch caution light is on whenever the actuator circuit is energised — engaging, disengaging or retensioning — and stays on until the belts are properly tensioned or completely disengaged.

Belt slack at engine start should be set so the blades begin turning within five seconds of clutch engagement; excessive slack can throw the belts out of the sheave grooves. A fuse on or near the test switch panel keeps an actuator motor overload from tripping the circuit breaker — if the fuse blows the motor stops but the caution light stays on. An open circuit breaker removes power from both the motor and the light, so no tensioning occurs and the light cannot indicate an abnormal condition.
sections.note: Never take off while the clutch caution light is on.

notes.title: Fuel System
notes.subtitle: A gravity-flow system with no fuel pumps — a main tank, an optional higher-mounted interconnected auxiliary tank, a shutoff valve behind the left seat, and a gascolator.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Fuel System).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: The fuel system is gravity-flow — there are no fuel pumps. It is a main tank, an optional auxiliary tank, a shutoff valve control behind the left seat, and a gascolator strainer on the lower left of the firewall. Later aircraft use flexible bladder tanks in aluminium enclosures; earlier aircraft use all-aluminium tanks. Tank air vents are inside the mast fairing.

The auxiliary tank is interconnected with the main tank and sits slightly higher, so it empties first while fuel still remains in the main tank; the shutoff valve controls flow from both tanks to the engine.

sections.heading: Drains and indication
paragraphs: Plunger-style drain valves serve the gascolator and each tank sump, with plastic tubes to drain fuel overboard; fuel is sampled from all three locations before the first flight of the day and after refuelling to check for contamination and correct grade. The fuel gauges are electrically operated by float-type transmitters — at E the tanks hold only a small quantity of unusable fuel. The low fuel caution light is actuated by a separate electric sender on the bottom of the main tank, independent of the gauges.

notes.title: Electrical System
notes.subtitle: A 14-volt DC system on an alternator and a sealed lead-acid battery, a fused bypass that keeps the tachometers and clock alive with the battery switch off, and the alternator-control-unit reset for an ALT light.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Electrical System, Dual Tachometer).

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: A standard 14-volt DC system with an alternator and a sealed lead-acid battery (in the engine compartment or beneath the instrument console). The battery switch controls the battery relay that disconnects the battery from the system; a fuse-protected wire near the battery bypasses that relay so both tachometers and the clock keep receiving battery power with the battery switch off. The circuit breaker panel is on the ledge forward of the left seat, and inflight reset of circuit breakers is not recommended. Later aircraft add an avionics master switch for the avionics bus.

sections.heading: Alternator monitoring
paragraphs: The alternator control unit protects the system from overvoltage. The ammeter shows current to the battery, with '−' indicating discharge. An ALT caution light or an ammeter discharge indication in flight means low voltage and possible alternator failure: turn off non-essential electrical equipment, switch the alternator off then back on after one second to reset the alternator control unit, and if the light stays on or the ammeter still shows discharge, land as soon as practical. Continued flight without a functioning alternator can lose power to the tachometers, which is a hazardous condition. Except for emergency procedures, the alternator should not be operated with the battery switched off — the battery helps protect equipment from voltage spikes.
sections.note: The electronic dual tachometer takes its engine signal from the magneto breaker points and its rotor signal from two magnetic senders at the main gearbox drive yoke, each on its own circuit breaker. With battery and alternator switches off, the tachometers still draw from the battery through the bypass as long as the clutch actuator switch is engaged — so the helicopter must not be stowed with the clutch switch engaged or the battery will discharge.

notes.title: Warning Lights, Audio Alerts and the EMU
notes.subtitle: The warning and caution lights and what drives each, the 97% low-RPM horn and 110% high-RPM warble, and the Engine Monitoring Unit whose flash rate tells the crew whether it has seen an exceedance.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Warning and Caution Lights, Audio Alerts, Engine Monitoring Unit).

sections.heading: Warning and caution lights
paragraphs: The lights are clutch, main gearbox over-temperature, main and tail gearbox chip, starter on (later aircraft), low fuel, low RPM, alternator, low oil pressure, rotor brake, governor off, carbon monoxide (aircraft with a cabin heater), and full throttle (later aircraft). The CLUTCH light indicates the clutch actuator is operating. The LOW RPM light and horn indicate rotor RPM at 97% or below. The low oil pressure and low fuel lights come from their own sensors, independent of the gauges. The ALT light warns of a possible alternator failure, and the GOV OFF light indicates the RPM governor is switched off.

The main and tail gearbox chip detectors are magnetic devices in each gearbox drain plug — metallic particles drawn to the magnet close the circuit and light the caution, giving warning of an impending gearbox failure. The main gearbox over-temp light comes from a temperature switch near the input pinion; the FULL THROTTLE light from a switch in the throttle linkage; the CARBON MONOXIDE light from a sensor above the pilot's heater outlet.

sections.heading: Audio alerts
paragraphs: Every R22 has a low-RPM horn that sounds below 97% rotor RPM and is muted with the collective fully down — through a console speaker on earlier aircraft, through the headsets on later aircraft. Later aircraft add a high-RPM warble (high/low tone) through the headsets as rotor RPM approaches 110%, with a panel test button. Optional equipment can add further headset alerts such as terrain and traffic warnings.

sections.heading: Engine Monitoring Unit
paragraphs: Later aircraft have an Engine Monitoring Unit — a digital recorder inside the RPM governor control box — that continuously logs engine and rotor speed, engine oil temperature, cylinder head temperature, manifold pressure, ambient pressure and OAT. Its status shows on an amber light in the right-side baggage compartment on the aft seat support panel. After the roughly ten-second self-test following battery-on, steady illumination means normal operation; a slow flash (once every two seconds) or no light means a fault in its senders or circuitry; a fast flash (four times per second) means it has detected an exceedance. Data downloads to a computer, and a fault or exceedance must be investigated and reset by a mechanic before the next flight. The EMU is a maintenance aid only — reporting observed exceedances remains the pilot's responsibility.

notes.title: Cabin Heating, Ventilation and CO Detector
notes.subtitle: Door and nose fresh-air vents, an optional muffler-shroud cabin heater with an overboard discharge, and a carbon-monoxide detector fitted only when the heater is.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Cabin Heating and Ventilation, Carbon Monoxide Detector).

sections.heading: Heating and ventilation
paragraphs: Fresh-air vents are in each door and in the nose. Door vents open and close with a knob near the hinge and lock either by pushing the knob in (earlier aircraft) or with a rotating knob (later); for maximum ventilation they open wide in the hover but only an inch or less in cruise. The nose inlet opens with the cabin air knob on the console face and directs air along the inside of the windshield for defogging as well as ventilation.

The cabin heater is optional: a muffler heat shroud, a control valve at the firewall, an outlet grille forward of the tail rotor pedals, and ducting. A heater control knob on the ledge forward of the pilot's seat drives the valve, directing heat either into the cabin or out an overboard discharge on the cabin underside. Earlier aircraft have an electric blower with its own switch; later aircraft take heater air from the engine cooling shroud and need no blower.
sections.note: In an in-flight engine fire, the heater control knob is pushed off to seal the cabin from the engine compartment.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide detector
paragraphs: The CO detector is fitted only if the optional cabin heater is installed. Carbon monoxide is an odourless toxic gas in engine exhaust; cabin levels can rise from an exhaust leak or from exhaust recirculation during prolonged hovering. The system is a sensor above the pilot's heater outlet plus a caution light. A system check (the light flashes twice) runs each time power is switched on; a continuing flash every four seconds indicates a sensor malfunction.

If the caution light illuminates: shut off the heater and open the nose and door vents to ventilate the cabin; if hovering, land or transition to forward flight; if symptoms of CO poisoning (headache, drowsiness, dizziness) accompany the light, land immediately, and have the exhaust system inspected before the next flight.

notes.title: Landing Gear and Rotor Brake
notes.subtitle: Skid gear that absorbs most landings elastically but yields the crosstube in an extreme one — replaced when the tail skid comes within 34 inches (24 for Standard/HP) of the ground — and an optional main-gearbox rotor brake with a 30-second wait and a 20-second minimum stop.
notes.rfmReference: R22 POH Section 7 (Systems Description — Landing Gear, Rotor Brake).

sections.heading: Landing gear
paragraphs: A skid-type landing gear. Most hard landings are absorbed elastically, but in an extremely hard landing the struts hinge up and outward as the crosstube yields (becomes permanently bent) to absorb the impact. Slight crosstube yielding is acceptable; yielding that brings the tail skid within 34 inches of the ground (24 inches for the R22 Standard or HP) with the helicopter empty on level pavement requires crosstube replacement. Abrasion-resistant wear shoes on the skid bottoms are replaced when the thinnest point in the wear area is less than 0.05 inches (1.3 mm).

sections.heading: Rotor brake
paragraphs: If installed, the rotor brake is on the aft end of the main gearbox, actuated by a cable to a pull handle above and behind the pilot's left shoulder. To stop the rotor: after pulling the mixture off, wait at least 30 seconds, then pull the handle forward and down with moderate force (about 10 lb); once the rotor stops, it can be used as a parking brake by hooking the bead chain in the bracket slot. The brake must be released before starting the engine, and while engaged it disables the starter. Applying the brake without waiting at least 30 seconds after the engine stops, or with a force that stops the rotor in less than 20 seconds, may damage the brake shoes.
